property_summary: After calling addToBalance with value x twice from the same caller, the stored balance (getBalance) is at least the sum of those two deposits.
After two deposits from the same caller, the recorded balance for that caller in C is at least the sum of the two deposits.
After making two deposits from this test contract, the recorded balance in C for this contract is at least the sum of the two deposits.
After calling addToBalance twice from this test contract, the recorded balance in C for this contract must be at least the sum of the two deposits.
After making two deposits from this test contract, the recorded balance in C for this contract is at least the sum of the two deposits.

Invariant: after any caller invokes addToBalance() with some wei, the caller's stored userBalance equals the previous balance plus the sent value; the mutant that sets balance to msg.value instead breaks this because it drops prior balance when msg.sender had nonzero balance.

Invariant: after any single call to addToBalance by any user, the caller's userBalance is equal to the amount they just sent (i.e., balances never decrease during that call); the mutated modifier that unlocks before the body allows a reentrant fallback to withdraw and thus can make some address's balance differ.

For any caller and any amount, after a single external addToBalance call by that caller, the total sum of all userBalance entries (observed as contract balance) equals address(c).balance — the buggy modifier permits reentrant withdrawals during addToBalance causing the internal mapping to be drained while on-chain balance remains, breaking the invariant that contract balance equals sum of stored balances.

For any attacker address A and any deposit amount v > 0, if A calls addToBalance{value: v} through a reentrant attacker helper that reenters on receive(), then after addToBalance returns the stored userBalance[A] in the correct contract equals the ETH that A contributed (i.e. userBalance for the attacker includes the deposit and cannot be reduced by reentrant withdrawals during the deposit); the buggy modifier that resets the lock early allows the attacker to reenter and reduce its stored balance, violating this property for some (A,v).

For any depositor and any nonzero deposit amount sent via addToBalance (possibly routed through a reentrant attacker helper), the contract's stored userBalance for the depositor after addToBalance returns is at least the amount they just sent (the buggy modifier that resets the lock early can enable reentrant withdraws during deposit and make the stored balance for some address smaller than the deposit).

For any two distinct addresses A (depositor) and B (attacker helper) and any deposit v>0 by A routed through B's payable entry that reenters to withdraw during the deposit, the reference contract ensures that after addToBalance returns, the stored balance of B is unchanged (i.e., B.userBalance(B) equals whatever it was before), while the mutant that unlocks before executing the body allows reentrant withdraw to reduce B's stored balance for some inputs.

For any caller and any wei amount, calling addToBalance increases the contract's stored balance for that caller by exactly msg.value (i.e., post-call userBalance(caller) == pre-call userBalance(caller) + amount); the mutant that zeroes the balance breaks this (some inputs show no net increase).

For every address u, getBalance(u) returns exactly the stored userBalance[u]; the mutant that returns userBalance[u] + userBalance[u] violates this because for any u with nonzero balance it returns double the correct value.

For any address u, C.getBalance(u) returns the stored userBalance[u]; the mutant that always returns 0 violates this because there exist addresses with non-zero stored balances for which getBalance(u) != 0.

For any address u, getBalance(u) always returns the stored userBalance for that address (i.e., userBalance[u]); the mutant instead returns userBalance[msg.sender], so for calls where msg.sender != u the mutant can return a different value and thus violates the rule.

For any caller and any eth amount, after calling addToBalance the caller's recorded userBalance equals the sum of previous balance and sent value (no external reentrancy can alter it during the call); removing the nonReentrant_ guard allows a reentrant attacker to disturb balances so this invariant can be broken for some inputs.

For any caller and any amount, immediately after addToBalance returns the caller's recorded userBalance equals the prior balance plus the sent value; removing the nonReentrant_ guard allows a reentrant caller to re-enter addToBalance during execution and change the stored balance so this equality can be violated for some adversarial caller/amount.

For any attacker address and deposit amount, after calling addToBalance through a malicious contract that re-enters during its receive(), the reference C (with nonReentrant_ on addToBalance) ensures the final stored userBalance for the attacker equals previous + sent value (no reentrant double-count), whereas the mutant (without nonReentrant_) can be re-entered to cause the recorded balance to be larger than expected for some fuzzed amounts and attacker addresses.

For any attacker contract and any nonzero deposit amount, calling addToBalance through an adversarial contract that REVERTs on receiving funds cannot change the recorded userBalance on revert in the reference (nonReentrant_ prevents state change when an external call reverts during addToBalance), whereas removing nonReentrant_ allows the mutant to have inconsistent state when the external call fails (some inputs cause balance to be updated despite the external revert).

For every caller and deposit amount, performing addToBalance must never allow the contract's address(this).balance to exceed the sum of all recorded userBalance values (i.e., contract ETH held equals sum of per-user balances); removing the nonReentrant_ on addToBalance permits reentrant manipulation so some inputs (attacker address / amount) make address(c).balance > sum of userBalance entries.

For any caller and any deposited amount, calling addToBalance with value X always increases that caller's stored balance by X (i.e., balance after == balance before + X) in the reference; the mutated modifier inverts the lock and can cause addToBalance to not update the stored balance for some inputs (depending on lock state), violating this rule.

For any caller and any deposit amount, a successful call to addToBalance increases that caller's stored balance by exactly the deposited amount (balance_after == balance_before + amount); the mutated modifier can invert the lock so addToBalance may not perform the update for some inputs, violating this invariant.

For any externally owned caller and any nonzero deposit amount, calling addToBalance from an EOA always increases that caller's stored userBalance by the deposited amount; the mutant's inverted lock can cause the call to be skipped (no increase) for some sequences/inputs, violating this rule.

For any caller and any deposit amount, a call to addToBalance that executes should always increase that caller's stored userBalance by the deposited amount (i.e., getBalance(after) == getBalance(before) + amount); the mutant's inverted nonReentrant_ lock can cause the update to be skipped for some inputs, violating this rule.

For any caller address and any deposit amount, calling addToBalance twice in sequence (two separate transactions) always results in the contract's recorded balance for that caller equaling the sum of the two deposits in the correct contract; the mutant's inverted lock can cause the second call to be blocked/skipped so the recorded balance is not the sum.

For any caller and any deposited amount, after withdrawBalance() returns the caller's recorded balance in the contract is zero (reference preserves zeroing-after-withdraw), but the mutant that zeroes after the external call can leave the contract's stored balance non-zero when the callee re-enters or the external call misbehaves.

For any depositor and any deposit amount, after a depositor calls withdrawBalance(), the contract's recorded userBalance for that depositor is zero (the reference always clears balance so getter returns 0); the mutant that zeros after the external call can leave a non-zero recorded balance when the callee is a reentrant attacker that re-enters during the external call.

For any depositor and any deposit amount, if a malicious recipient re-enters during withdrawBalance's external call the reference contract always results in address(c).balance decreased by the withdrawn amount (i.e., no extra Ether remains in the contract after a successful withdraw), whereas the mutant that zeroes after the external call can be drained/left with a larger-than-expected contract balance due to reentrancy and thus violates that invariant for some inputs.

After calling withdrawBalance, the caller's recorded balance in the reference C is guaranteed to be zero (the contract clears the balance after sending funds); the mutant that omits zeroing can leave the caller's balance nonzero, violating this rule for some inputs.

After a successful withdrawBalance call, the caller's recorded userBalance in the reference contract is always zero; the mutant that omits zeroing the balance can leave it non-zero when the external call succeeds.

Invariant: after a successful withdrawBalance call by any user, that user's balance in the contract becomes zero (reference C always sets userBalance[msg.sender] = 0 after the external call); the buggy mutant that removed lock clearing allows a reentrant attacker to re-enter withdraw and drain funds so that this invariant can be violated for some inputs.

For every caller and deposit amount, after withdrawBalance() returns successfully the caller's userBalance in C is zero; removing the lock unset allows a reentrant attacker to make withdrawBalance() return while leaving a nonzero userBalance for some inputs (attacker and amounts).

For any attacker-deployed contract and any nonzero deposit amount, if the attacker deposits and then calls withdrawBalance(), the reference C always ends with the attacker’s recorded userBalance == 0 after withdraw returns; the mutant (which omits resetting the reentrancy lock) can be exploited by a reentrant attacker contract to have withdrawBalance() return while leaving a nonzero userBalance for some fuzzed amounts/attacker addresses.

For any attacker contract address A and deposit amount v>0, if A deposits v and then calls withdrawBalance(), the reference C always ends with address(c).balance decreased by v (i.e., contract funds are transferred out) and A's recorded userBalance == 0 after withdraw returns; the mutant that removes unlocking in the modifier can be reentered so withdrawBalance() can return while leaving a nonzero recorded userBalance and thus not actually reducing address(c).balance by the full expected amount for some attacker/amount combinations.

For any attacker contract A and deposit amount v>0, if A deposits v and then calls withdrawBalance(), then after withdrawBalance() returns the contract's stored userBalance for A is zero (reference preserves this for all inputs); the mutant that removes unlocking of the reentrancy guard allows a reentrant attacker to cause withdrawBalance() to return while leaving a nonzero recorded userBalance for some attacker/address and amount, violating the rule.

After withdrawBalance returns, the caller's recorded balance in the reference contract is always zero (the reference always zeroes the caller's userBalance after sending funds), whereas the mutant that zeroes before the external call can result in non-zero recorded balance for some user due to reentrant behaviour by a malicious recipient.

For any attacker address A and deposit amount v, after A deposits v and then calls withdrawBalance(), the reference contract C always has userBalance(A) == 0 afterwards; the mutant that zeroes balance before the external transfer can be reentered by a malicious recipient so there exist inputs (attacker address and deposit) where userBalance(A) != 0 after withdraw, violating the rule.

For any attacker address A and deposit v > 0, after A deposits v and then calls withdrawBalance(), the reference C guarantees that no OTHER user's balance increases as a result (i.e., withdraw cannot be used to transfer funds from A to some other user); the mutant that zeroes the caller balance before the external call can be reentered to move funds into another user's balance, violating this invariant for some inputs.

For any depositor A and any attacker contract Att that can re-enter, after A deposits v and A calls withdrawBalance() routed through Att, the reference C ensures that the map entry userBalance(another) for any unrelated address B never increases as a result of A's withdraw; the mutant can be re-entered to credit a different address B, so there exist fuzzed A, B, v, and Att where userBalance(B) increases in the mutant but not in the reference.

For every attacker contract address A and deposit amount v, after A deposits v and then calls withdrawBalance(), the reference C always leaves the caller's recorded userBalance(A) equal to 0; the mutant that zeroes before the external call can be re-entered so there exist A and v where userBalance(A) != 0 after withdraw, breaking the invariant.

For every caller and amount, calling withdrawBalance on the reference never lets a reentrant attacker steal funds from another user's userBalance (i.e., after withdrawBalance completes, total userBalance for any key is unchanged except for the caller's balance which is zeroed by withdrawal); removing nonReentrant_ allows a reentrant contract to reenter withdrawBalance and cause another key's userBalance to be drained, violating this invariant.
